title: "Art House" films that are comfort films for you?

commenti.body: [removed]

Hagazussa. It's terrifying and quite strange, but there are some beautiful introspective moments. I watched it for the first time last week and I completely fell in love with the atmosphere and slower pace that allows the horror to develop.

Paris, Texas; Close Up; A Moment of Innocence; Uncle Boonmee; First Cow

Red Shoes doesn't really count as arthouse but ill throw it in

First Cow, Paris,Texas, and Uncle Boonmee are just incredibly relaxing and very pretty films and ill usually tear up at some point but in a good way - they all have that nice fuzziness which is why I set them aside as a group
Does The Florida Project count? If so, The Florida Project. Absolutely stunning beautiful film with not outright leisurely, but manageable pacing, and a very realistic world established.

I can echo that sentiment about Stalker of how it gradually settles you in to its detached, spaced-out atmosphere. With art in general, I've always adored works that feel as if they were created solely as a paean to joy itself--that want nothing else but to express their happiness at being happy. Their fervent, infectious energy is not only invigorating for me, but oddly comforting at the same time. Shakespeare's "A Midsummer Night's Dream" is a classic example that comes to mind. For films, Wong Kar-Wai's earlier works like "Chungking Express," and "Fallen Angels" also give me that same warm impression. Some of Kusturica's films like "Black Cat, White Cat," "Underground," and "Arizona Dream" do the same as well ("Time of the Gypsies" is way too haunting to qualify though).

"Smoke" from 1995. Here's part of a rotten tomato's review: "poignant art-house movie about melancholic characters with uplifting stories who like nothing better than telling a story and having a smoke." It's kind of a slow burn (pun intended) but  is the type of movie I like to watch if I'm home and not feeling well or just a lazy afternoon type of movie.

I shudder at the idea of films being 'background' but I know what you mean about Barry Lyndon: it's a soothing and immersive film. 

As for comfort films: really it's anything by Kore-eda. His films are so gentle and quiet: the small and intimate details of families preparing meals or walks in the local park become gorgeously realised studies of life in modern Japan. He elevates the mundane to the profound in the subtle way great painters can.

Mulholland Drive. I’ve seen it dozens of times. What does it mean? I don’t know. But it’s so beautiful and inspires the viewer to wonder. It’s pre-multiverse and you never know if the characters are already dead.
Love that film. Barely any dialogue, but it's so beautifully shot.

Lynch is definitely one of the best at creating a sense of atmosphere. He may even be the best. That infamous jump-scare, where you’re told exactly how it’s going to play out, yet it still manages to work disturbingly well, because Lynch makes you feel like you’re stuck in a nightmare and helplessly moving forward to an inevitable culmination of dread waiting for you to confront it.

Solaris - meditative and introspective,  it’s like a waking dream that lingers and purposefully unfolds at a snails pace. 

It is poetic and artistic, everything feels like a moving painting. 

The way it just ponders itself is amazing to watch. 

It is so very tranquil, even when at times quite melancholic and dark. 

As with all of Tarkovsky’s work it is all a celebration of life and it’s unknowable wonder. No matter how dark he goes everything has a beauty to it. 

Couldn’t care less how cheap it looks, actually makes the whole thing more human. Also allows you to focus on the emotions of the characters and the story. 

It is a direct challenge to a film like 2001, a Hollywood masterpiece that is cold and heartless. Tarkovsky asks similar existential questions but where as Kubrick is looking at humanity at large Tarkovsky takes on the individual. 

I love the main character in the film and his mix of boyhood curiosity mixed with the cynicism and snark of an adult who has experienced much trauma. 

The film just feels alive and I can put it on whenever and just meditate to its natural beauty. Who needs shots of complex space stations when you can simply shoot seaweed flowing in the water. 

Also as someone who struggled accepting a break up and dealing with ‘losing’ that person forever this film was perfect. It is actually a very bittersweet romance film, or rather it’s the aftermath of a failed romance that is dissected on screen. 

It can be very hard to watch only because it’s so relatable in parts in terms of trying to hold onto the past and the damage it does to you. 

There is a catharsis in the end with moving on, and I feel like I’ve just attended a very abstract performative art therapy session.

Mike Leigh's *Naked*, for some reason lol. Not sure why or what that says about me. I guess part of it is I just love the way he captured the atmosphere of a nocturnal London underbelly. It's one of those films where the city itself almost feels like it's part of the cast. Also there is something to it like what you said of *Stalker*, that the bleak, wounded melancholy of it is somehow soothing once you're familiar with the film.

One that always soothes me is D'est by Chantal Akerman (I think it translates to "From the East" or something like that). There's not really any dialogue, and what soothes me is that there's a bunch of very long shots of just...people, going about their lives. The setting is the collapse of the Soviet Union, specifically in Poland/East Germany/Ukraine. It's also just damn interesting, I notice something new every time!  Especially in the scenes where it's just lines of people waiting for the train/bus.
In the Mood for love for me, I’ve seen it plenty of times and just having it on in the background while I’m reading can be pretty comforting. I like the soundtrack/score a lot so that helps.
I was going to say Uncle Boonmee. Apichatpong has even said that he’s okay with people sleeping during his films since he sees them as being adjacent to dreaming (don’t remember his exact wording).

I rarely rewatch movies, but I've seen The Lighthouse quite a few times. It was the movie that got my 18 year old self into "weird" movies, and it still resonates with me on a deep level. I prefer not to think about what the fact that The Lighthouse is one of my most rewatched movie says about me though, let's not open that door.
Not sure if it counts as Art House but Waking Life... I used to fall asleep to it when I was in my early twenties. It would feed my soul and help me to sleep. To me it's a perfect film.

That whole scene was horrifying not just because of the context of why she was eating, but it just made me so sad for the hell she'd been put through.
I love having Mulholland Drive on in the background. With its dreamlike structure and gorgeous cinematography, it feels right to drop in and out of watching it.

Unsure if these count as "arthouse" but a lot of Jim Jarmusch's do this for me, Stranger Than Paradise, Down by Law, Coffee & Cigarettes, etc. Something about the pacing and the rhythm of the dialogue is just relaxing to me-- it's sometimes slow but somehow has enough intrigue to never be boring. It's like listening to your Token Cool Friend tell a good story
I completely forgot about him. Dead Man and even Ghost Dog do the same for me as well.

There's more than a handful of reasons why Paris, Texas is my all-time favorite movie. Everything about it is beautiful, the story, the photograph, Ry Cooder's brilliant score. It's just exquisite all around, and man it hits those heartstrings as well.

5 Centimeters Per Second (2007).  The hushed sounds, poetic dialogue, the gorgeous artwork and wistful story make for such and comforting film experience. This is the very definition of comfort film.   
The Boy and the Heron (2023) I just saw this and have been listening to the soundtrack all day. It’s a sad story about loss and death told through a fantasy adventure where Miyazaki references previous imagery making very familiar. It’s a deeply comfortable movie.   
The Green Ray (1986) Rohmer makes deeply comfortable movies. In general, his films have lovers navigate the difficulties of love and relationships in healthy non combative ways which is very refreshing. This movie is for introverts and is very comforting as such.

Wenders’ other movies are very cozy for me as well, particularly Kings of the Road and Alice in the Cities, and his documentary Tokyo-Ga. Not plot-driven, not much overt conflict, mostly just vibes. 

Weerasathatkul is similar—his movies are perfect for watching while dozing off on the couch on a Sunday afternoon (but of course also deserve to be watched properly too.)

To this day, I have no idea what is and isn't art house. But here's mine anyway.

Mike Leigh: *Life is Sweet*, *Career Girls*, and *Happy-Go-Lucky*

Kelly Reichardt: *Old Joy*

Hirokazu Kore-eda: *Our Little Sister*

Jim Jarmusch: *Paterson*

Not sure if it counts but probably Taxi Driver. It's something that I can put on and be in absolute awe at the depth and genius that exists in filmmaking.

Honourable mentions that are popping into my mind:

- Requiem for a Dream

- The Killing of a Sacred Deer

- Cure

- Safe (1995)

Until now, only Close Up by Abbas Kiaroostami comfort me the most. The fact its a pretty light story, i could stare at the screen watching nothing and thinking nothing lol. The slow pace, simple cinematography, Score-less, and the light story of this film makes no urge focus, just vibing, and when the cilmax is reached, when they started to talk deep, you realize ayo this is getting real. Score slowly appearing, accompanying us to the end of the story.

Vertical Ray of the Sun: from Vietnam this is a visually beautiful film. The film opens with Lou Reed over a brother and sister waking up in their sun drenched 2nd floor apartment and follows their family from there. It is a story of love triangles  and questions of family secrets. Nothing feels too consequential yet it is a meditation on family life in Vietnam. Watch this one.

Antonioni’s *The Passenger* or *Zabriskie Point* and Wim Wender’s *The American Friend*, two priemier art house directors’ foray into genre films that walk a fine line between their usual schtick and the dynamism and suspense of thrillers - can be enjoyed without being too intellectually engaged lol, I put these on periodically just for the gorgeous visuals

smoke was filmed in my hood in Brooklyn Windsor Terrace and Park slope. They shot over the summer of 1995 . I even shot some video on their wrap day. He actually shot two films since he came in way under budget with smoke … the other film shot concurrently is Blue in the face. So cool seeing all the cameos in that film from Michael J Fox to Madonna.  Another film that was shot on the same blocks was As Good as it gets . I was blown away to see Jack Nicholson for over 2 weeks just hanging out in the hood.

I honestly don't care for the label "Art House". I don't think it means anything and it's such a vast spectrum of films. I think those so called "Art House" movies could fall into different, distinct genres. I think a better label is contemplative cinema, Cinema that pauses and stops to smell the roses. Anyway, I would say a favorite of mine is Gates of Heaven. That movie is like a warm blanket for me, it's basically a unhurried look at life itself and different POVs of what lays beyond this mortal plane. Another one, I would argue, is the John Huston film Beat The Devil. That's really the only Hollywood film you will ever see that truly depends on the charm of it's actors/characters and it's breezy observations about how foolish society is brings me joy. The target is the British Empire but it can apply to those who simply value material wealth.
That's cool!

I've seen plenty of movies I would call "art house" that are absolutely not slow or contemplative, though. And I don't think there's anything wrong with a label that's very broad, as long as it's still covering a vaguely recognizable group, which I believe "art house" does

I think it's tossed around far too liberally to the point where it has lost all meaning. I honestly feel that it should be something specific: Something provocative, typically not hurried, and outside a traditional narrative structure.

I love Tarkovsky and Mike Leigh but damned if I find their movies comforting.

again, not sure what counts as "art house", but there's this chinese movie, Oxhide 2, that's 2h+ of just a family preparing and eating dumplings in real time, composed of something like 9 15-ish minute long static shots, and i love it so much. Watching it kinda made me understand for the first time why people enjoy watching livestreamers on twitch

Anything by Tsai Ming-liang. His films can be very dark in their subject matter, but the way they're shot and edited makes them comforting. They're very slow-paced, even meditatively so. The camera might linger for minutes on shot before anything happens. In that sense, he's quite similar to Bála Tarr. 

They also often feature slow and intimate interactions between characters that feel soothing to watch. 

Though afterwards, I usually feel sadness or shock, or combination of both.
Wouldn’t Fellini’s work fall into this? Or are his films too sad and bittersweet for that?
I just love doing this with movies in general! It’s an attention span thing too though, I shouldn’t lie, lmao.
The ending is tough. I often turn it off before then.

I can see what you mean with his sense of whimsy and playfulness. Someone like Wes Anderson is definitely like that as well. His stuff imo always does have a element of sadness lurking behind everything. It makes for deeper films though. The closest thing for me would be Satyiricon, but there's a perverse darkness to it too (which is a film I overall love).

Right right right. I wanted to mention yeah, I guess in the first half of the film, especially the scenes with the women characters, it IS much more dreamlike, without that like, noir-ish, nightmare horror element there just yet.

Oh yeah, so funnily enough, Satyricon was the FIRST Fellini I watched, which is interesting since 

1.) it’s not usually seen as his top tier work. 

2.) it’s VERY surreal in a way his most acclaimed stuff also isn’t, to my understanding. 

La Dolce Vita is grounded in realism, 8 1/2 is some in between between fantasy and reality, and Amacord is pure comedy, rather than comedy drama, at least from what I’ve seen of it. 

But yeah, I remember Satryricon being quite dark and fantastical! And yeah, perverse too, in a way like, a Tim Burton movie just isn’t, since that’s too aimed at children (which is fine!)

Terry gilliams stuff, from my understanding, is closer to the adult, surreal fantasy of Satyricon.
Miyazaki's Ponyo is one of my favorite films for a similar reason. It's overflowing with such a strong sense of pure childlike joy that is extremely comforting and even inspiring for me.

I agree. Even something like Totoro, which does have a lot of whimsy, has a sliver of sadness underlying everything, but Ponyo seemed like Miyazaki at his most gleeful.

Haven't seen it mentioned yet so *Yi Yi* by Edward Yang. I feel cleansed when I watch it. The narcissism inherent in anxiety and depressive spiraling seems to be dispelled and I am reminded that life is much bigger than myself. It's the perfect movie. 

Not sure if it's necessarily a comfort film for me but *Taste of Cherry* and most Kiarostami movies are nice to put on in the background. I want to fall asleep to them, which I think Kiarostami would agree is a good thing.
Oh yes! One of my favorites!

The thing about Hollywood comfort films - is that Hollywood can’t live without conflict, so their comfort films are actually just something trivial enough to not worry about while still being filled with conflict.

An actual comfort film would almost by definition be arthouse.

And so:

Michelangelo Frammartino’s comforting anthropological documentary fictions: Il Buco and Le quattro volte

Koreeda’s Our Little Sister

The Slovak New Wave’s Celebration in the Botanical Garden and Birds, Orphans, and Fools (the latter opening to tell you that it ends tragically but not to worry about it)

Sokurov’s Days of Eclipse, Mother and Son, Father and Son, and Whispering Pages

I used to have a longer list but I lost it…
Arguably there are several livestreams that really blow Oxhide 2 out of the water. Under appreciated gems.
